questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was crucial for me that the location had courses that lined up (in terms of relevance) with what I’m doing back home and that it felt like I wasn’t just wasting ects points. It was also important to me that it was a predominantly English speaking country, as I think it would have been too overwhelming to both have 4 full courses and have to learn a new language to complete those courses. Another personal reason for my choice of Canada, was that it both feels somewhat similar but also very different to us culturally. This meant that I had a lot of new aspects to explore of the culture, but I didn’t struggle to find people to relate to either. It was nice to be able to blend in a bit once in a while. The access to both nature and bigger cities is also great here, which was something I was looking for too.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I feel that the stress of wanting to do well was a little overwhelming at times and sadly took my focus of off just enjoying the experience to the fullest. This was mainly due to the fact that there are no options for re-examination and I didn’t feel very informed about what would happen in case of a failed exam or course. It takes some time to feel secure academically in a new system even if you do well, because you have to align yourself to new standards and expectations. Besides from this though it has been a huge learning experience and I’ve met lots of wonderful people throughout my stay. So I have no regrets of going!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy! McMaster did a wonderful job of assisting exchange students both online and in person, beforehand and during. They for example had exchange buddies you could reach out to, and people from the university waiting at the airport to help you figure out how to get to your place and/or campus with the transport systems they have. They also did a exchange orientation which provided good opportunity for asking questions and meeting a lot of the other exchange students. Their websites could be a little confusing at times, but you could always reach out to representatives on phone or email if you were unsure about any of the information needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As mentioned in the previous question there was the exchange orientation. Here we could sign up for different things like getting help with speaking and/or writing in English, or different clubs that would do events throughout the term etc. We also got some general information about where to get medical assistance if needed and much more. Generally they provided us with all the tools necessary for thriving. The only thing I might have wished for was a map of the different buildings on campus, but that was possible to find online if you looked up the specific buildings and the university’s name.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was not super easy, as there is a high demand in housing in the area in general, driving up the prices. I was able to find a place that was relatively cheap and solely for students around 25 minutes from campus. I would recommend being careful when looking on your own though, as I did hear of people that had been scammed. So make sure to get proper contact with the landlord, get a tour if possible and get a proper contract from them. There are a lot of rooms for rent available, but some can be quite far away or have strict rules like no guest (the latter supposedly isn’t even legal, but people put it up as a criteria anyways). So a recommendation is to start looking early, but also be aware that if you start very early there probably won’t be much as they will be renting it out for the semester before you arrive. So lookout for something early and continuously if you want to find the best option for yourself.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It can be tough at times. You have to be prepared for some possible hurdles. I would recommend finding out early with your bank and landlord how to set up rent payment, as it gives some comfort not having to worry about how to make the payments. It can also feel a little isolating at times if the other people you live with already have very established lives and don’t seek out social interactions in the house. It often does pay off to get to know them though. Also make sure to get proper contact information from your landlord. I was in the unlucky situation of a power outage during a holiday where I couldn’t get in contact with my landlord and didn’t have any power in my room for 3 days, except for in my fridge because it ran on a different power source. In retrospect it would have been nice to make sure to have a proper and updated emergency contact number for the landlord.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was so so. It could have been better, but it could definitely also have been much worse. I think it is a little bit about luck and knowing where to look to be honest.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was alright, though it required a lot of updating throughout the way as it wasn’t fully adjusted to international phone numbers etc.  It wasn’t super difficult, just a little tedious and time consuming at times.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
First there was the application for the university in which you had to do a letter explaining why you wanted to apply to McMaster and also attach your university’s confirmation of your exchange and a transcript of your grades. 
When this had been accepted you had to remember to accept the offer from McMaster.
Then you had to fill out a bunch of personal information, like home address and phone numbers for both yourself and emergency contacts. You also had to submit a photo for your student card. Remembering to update this information when you move to Canada and possibly change to a Canadian phone number is important. At this point you would already have received an email and password which had to be changed for security reasons, which would gain you access to an outlook email, mosaic and avenue2learn, which are their main student portals. Then you would have to make sure that you’re signed up for their healthcare program UHIP and enroll in the courses. The course enrolling happens in the summer, so be sure what courses you want to sign up for and have the pre-acceptance of them from UCPH before enrolling to make the process less stressful for yourself. It  should be possible to change and drop courses at McMaster later if necessary, but you can’t be guaranteed a course if it’s already filled etc. McMaster will update you through the email you first used for contact through UCPH, but will switch to your assigned email address from them later on, so keep an eye on both during the registration period.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Keeping close contact with both their exchange coordinators and the ones from UCPH, along with the contact person from your faculty at McMaster was helpful. They were the people I found myself needing to contact the most. Also read the guides they send you thoroughly! These guides have a lot of the information you need, like how to contact them and when different deadlines are.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful I’d say. Sadly some of the courses I initially wanted were for the wrong semester and a few of the ones I found interesting were overlapping. But I ended up finding more than enough that I found interesting to create a schedule for and register in.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make yourself a list of deadlines and set yourself goals and reminders for when to have specific parts of the process done, so you don’t get stressed out and have to do things last minute in case of problems. Make use of the contact information, but remember that there’s a time difference and that answers can take a couple of days at times.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a really good program and the professors where great at both teaching and helping out in case of confusion.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I was in my second year of my BA back home doing my exchange when I had my electives. I took three third year courses and one first year course. This seemed very fitting to my level, but that is also because I had chosen courses that were relevant and therefore extensions on my previous knowledge from home. The first year course was surprisingly the most tedious in my opinion, as they take into account that a lot of people are fresh out of high school in Canada when doing their first year. This meant that it was a much bigger class and they were a lot less lenient in the way they did assignments, tests and exams in terms of style compared to the third year courses. So third year classes is generally what I would recommend, just like they do. That being said, the first year course did come in handy as it provided very thorough guides on academic guidelines, and served as a prerequisite for some of my third year classes.
I would say it is important to make sure your feel confident not just in speaking English, but in writing it as well, as that makes up a large chunk of your grade in many courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It was structured quite differently.  Mainly because it had shorter lectures and then one tutorial for each course per week. Attendance is obviously important back at UCPH, but it is a part of your grade here and you need to actively participate to get full marks for attendance. They will (or at least should!
) make you aware of these expectations in the start of the course though. Generally the way they do final grades is very different as they grade you on your efforts throughout the semester, which means you don’t just get your exam grade like you would in a lot of courses at UCPH. So that is something to be prepared for.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ENVSOCTY 1HA3 - Society, Culture and Environment.
ENVSOCTY 3MA3 - Research Methods
ENVSOCTY 3UW3 - Cities of the Developing World
ENVIRSC 3B03 - Ecosystems and Global Change.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all of these courses, as I felt like they were all developing different skills of great interest to me. I do recommend the 3rd year courses more though, as I preferred the smaller class and the way they were taught in general.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Kitchenware and a few other things from IKEA like a drying rack etc. as the place I rented  didn’t have a sharing system in the kitchen and the dryers were the industrial kind which is no good for delicate fabrics. (I put 0.00kr in personal spendings and other fees as it is very hard to make up a consistent number per month and it doesn’t feel like it would it necessarily be very representative of the general experience.)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries, if choosing to buy organic some specific wares will be VERY expensive compared to back home. Yoghurt for example is almost the doubled price for organic compared to back home.
School textbooks are pretty expensive too, I had four and payed around 1600kr total, which doesn’t sound like much, but the two textbooks make up 1400kr of that total. Something that was surprisingly cheap though was bus transport which I heavily relied on. I payed nothing for it within Hamilton as McMaster provided a transit pass for free.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very satisfied! They had lots of clubs and sports events. Also they had a free gym with both lots of equipment and classes you could take for free too. Some cost money, but those were the ones you had to sign up for. Lots of smaller events hosted by clubs as well and even a free art gallery at the school too.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: An art gallery, a gym, sport events like basketball and volleyball etc., an end of the semester fair, club events like board game nights, quiz nights etc., and a lot of events specifically targeted towards exchange students and international students with ice skating, free dinners, hikes and much more. They even did an IKEA trip and such for the exchange students. They even had a planetarium and a small nuclear reactor that you could visit on campus.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely go to the free dinners for exchange students! It’s a wonderful way to meet the other exchange students and try some different kinds of food. I would also recommend just going to whatever you get the chance to go to, sports events were for example really fun to both watch and participate in, which is not something I would normally do much at home.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore the city! If you live in Hamilton specifically, it might seem like a bit of a dull city, but find some friends and go see the natural areas around, visit board game cafes, go to the local cinema (Westdale cinema is cute in particular!), explore and you will surely find something for your taste. Visit Toronto for sure! Maybe go to Niagara Falls if you get the chance. Even if you don’t want to spend a lot of money you can find many hidden gems. At the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto you can for example get a free year pass if your under 25. So yeah, just explore opportunities and ask other students (both local and other exchange and international  students) for tips and company on your trips!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy I’d say. People are very friendly, they even thank the bus driver on the busses in Hamilton. As long as you make the effort to be approachable and friendly, people return it happily and are super helpful. One thing that has been harder to adjust to is the amount of homeless people in Hamilton and Toronto. It can feel a little scary in the downtown areas at night as a lot of them are on hardcore drugs and can be very loud yelling at people and act quite weird at times in the streets. I haven’t personally experienced any problems with them though, despite living close to an area where a lot of them are settled. So it’s more so because it’s shocking how big of a problem it is there. Also the cities are extremely car oriented, so going on bike or foot can sometimes be challenging or a little daunting in some areas as it’s not always super pedestrian friendly. But there are still areas that are more suitable for walking and biking as well!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It might seem awkward or challenging to initiate contact, but from my experience people are very excited to talk! Try and be open to opportunities, be the first to say hi and introduce yourself to people you sit next to in class. Don’t be afraid to ask for people’s social media or phone numbers when having talked, especially if you’ve mentioned that your an exchange student people will be very happy to help you with things and show you places in the city!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There weren’t really any cultural differences I found challenging to be honest. I actually found that people were easier to get to know here than back home to some degree! People are very open and friendly if you try your best to be so.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Again, the friendly people! I for example got invited to a girls family Easter dinner because she knew I obvious didn’t have my own family to celebrate it with here. So people really do their best to make sure you feel welcome and accepted.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Prepare as much as you can from home to reduce any stress, through being thorough in your planning and reading all of the guides that they provide.
2. Do your best to participate in activities on campus and outside of campus, it makes for really fun experiences even if it’s not something you’d normally do. So be curious and seek things out!
3. Don’t beat yourself up when things don’t go as expected or if you feel stressed out about schoolwork, it’s okay as it’s an learning experience and you just have to do the best you can! At times it can feel tough, but it’ll be worth it for all the good experiences you get along the way.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There can be unexpected fees and it is always good to have some savings to rely on. Familiarise yourself with the different contacts and student portals as early as possible to make life easier for yourself. And don’t be afraid to ask for help!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The experiences I have had with other people and the knowledge that I can handle things very well on my own even when it feels very challenging. I feel like it has made me much more independent and resourceful, and it has reassured me that being outgoing and open can get you a long way.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: All the administrative stuff both before and during the stay. Especially before as there are a lot of things that need to be planned ahead of time and a lot of uncertainties which can be scary. Also balancing doing schoolwork, having fun and relaxing can be hard if you get stressed out by schoolwork.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
